summary: Ceftriaxone is a long-acting third-generation cephalosporin given IV or IM for many serious bacterial infections, from pneumonia and meningitis to gonorrhea. Once-daily dosing suits most indications. Key safety issue: ceftriaxone-calcium precipitates, so it must not be mixed with calcium-containing IV fluids in neonates.

dosage.d: 1-2 g once daily (or divided q12h); max 4 g/day
dosage.n: Continue at least 2 days after symptoms resolve

dosage.d: Initial 100 mg/kg (max 4 g), then 100 mg/kg/day; max 4 g/day

admin: Give IV infusion over 30 minutes (over 60 minutes in neonates to reduce bilirubin encephalopathy risk)
Do NOT reconstitute or dilute with calcium-containing diluents (e.g., Ringer's, Hartmann's)
Do NOT co-administer with calcium-containing IV solutions in neonates
In non-neonates, ceftriaxone and calcium solutions may be given sequentially if line is thoroughly flushed
Do NOT give IV solutions containing lidocaine; lidocaine only as diluent for IM use
Obtain culture/susceptibility before starting when possible
moa: Beta-lactam that binds penicillin-binding proteins, inhibiting bacterial cell-wall (peptidoglycan) synthesis; bactericidal. Resistant to many beta-lactamases.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to ceftriaxone, its excipients, or any cephalosporin
Premature neonates up to post-menstrual age of 41 weeks
Hyperbilirubinemic neonates (ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from albumin -> bilirubin encephalopathy risk)
Neonates (<=28 days) requiring calcium-containing IV solutions (ceftriaxone-calcium precipitation risk)
relative: Prior hypersensitivity to penicillins/other beta-lactams (cross-reactivity risk)
History of GI disease, particularly colitis
Severe renal AND hepatic impairment combined
monitor: Diarrhea suggestive of C. difficile colitis
Prolonged therapy: CBC, hematologic and hepatic parameters

preg: No evidence of harm in animals; no adequate human studies. Use only if clearly needed.
lact: Low concentrations excreted in human milk; use with caution.
renal: No dosage adjustment usually needed; caution if severe renal AND hepatic impairment.
hepatic: No dosage adjustment usually needed; caution if severe renal AND hepatic impairment.

major: Calcium-containing IV solutions (precipitation, fatal in neonates)
interactions.diagnostics: May cause false-positive urine glucose (non-enzymatic methods) and false-positive Coombs test.

monitoring: Assess for penicillin/cephalosporin/beta-lactam allergy before first dose
Watch for hypersensitivity during and after administration
Monitor for diarrhea / signs of C. difficile colitis
Prolonged therapy: periodic CBC, renal and hepatic function
Neonates: avoid concurrent calcium-containing IV fluids; monitor bilirubin
counsel: Report rash, itching, swelling, or trouble breathing immediately
Report severe or watery/bloody diarrhea, even weeks after treatment
Tell clinician about all penicillin or cephalosporin allergies
pk: ~151 mcg/mL after 1 g IV (end of infusion)
Store dry powder per label; use reconstituted solution per stability instructions
pearls: Long half-life (~8 h) allows once-daily dosing in most infections.
Single 250 mg IM dose treats uncomplicated gonorrhea; add antichlamydial cover as it lacks activity against C. trachomatis.
Contraindicated in neonates needing calcium-containing IV fluids - ceftriaxone-calcium precipitates have caused fatal lung/kidney crystallization.
Hyperbilirubinemic and premature neonates must not receive it (bilirubin displacement -> encephalopathy).
Eliminated by both renal (33-67% unchanged) and biliary routes, so no routine dose change for renal OR hepatic impairment alone.
Not removed by hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis.
missed: Parenteral, clinician-administered; resume schedule as directed - do not double up.
overdose: Discontinue drug; supportive care. Not reduced by dialysis. Watch for neurological effects (encephalopathy, seizures), especially in renal impairment.
refs: U.S. FDA label via openFDA / DailyMed
